# 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms

Polynomial multiplication is the engine behind the next two chapters. This
chapter explains the contracts behind NTT, arbitrary-mod strategies, division, product
trees, evaluation, interpolation and Taylor shift.

## 1. Convolution and transforms

For $C(x)=A(x)B(x)$, $c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j$. Evaluating at sufficiently
many points turns multiplication into pointwise products; interpolation returns
the coefficients. FFT uses complex roots of unity, NTT roots in a finite field.

For transform length $L=2^{s}$, a prime modulus $p$ must satisfy $L\mid p-1$
and a primitive $L$th root must exist. With $998244353 = 119*2^{23}+1$, primitive
root $3$, lengths through $2^{23}$ are available.

### Transform contract

Complex FFT needs coefficient splitting and careful rounding. When the target
modulus is arbitrary, use enough NTT-friendly primes to reconstruct each integer
coefficient by CRT, then reduce modulo the target. The coefficient bound, not
the target modulus, determines how many primes are enough; three primes are only
a common choice when their product exceeds the proved bound. If only the result
modulo $m$ matters, Garner reconstruction can avoid a huge integer. AtCoder
Library's `convolution_ll` is a reliable reference for its stated signed-64-bit
coefficient range.

Complexity is $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ memory.

## 2. Polynomial division

If $\deg A<\deg B$, return $Q=0$ and $R=A$. Otherwise, let
$\operatorname{rev}_k(F)$ mean: reverse the full coefficient array of $F$,
then truncate or pad the result to length $k$.
For $A=BQ+R$, $\deg R<\deg B$, set $k=\deg(A)-\deg(B)+1$. Reversal gives

$$
 \operatorname{rev}_k(Q) \equiv
 \operatorname{rev}_k(A)\,\operatorname{rev}_k(B)^{-1}\pmod{x^k}.
$$

Compute the FPS inverse (chapter 07), reverse back, and set $R=A-BQ$. This costs
$O(M(n))$. Preconditions: field coefficients and nonzero leading coefficient.

## 3. Product tree, multipoint evaluation

For points $x_i$, build a balanced tree
$P_v(x)=\prod_{i\in v}(x-x_i)$. At the root compute `f mod P_root`; descend
with `remainder mod P_child`. At leaf $i$, the constant remainder is $f(x_i)$.
Fast division at every level yields $O(M(n)\log n)$.

Naive Horner is better when the degree or number of points is small; fast
algorithms have large constants.

## 4. Interpolation

For distinct $x_i$, let $P(x)=\prod_i(x-x_i)$. Lagrange basis gives

$$
f(x)=\sum_i y_i\frac{P(x)}{(x-x_i)P'(x_i)}.
$$

Evaluate $P'$ at all points with the product tree. Put
$w_i=y_i/P'(x_i)$ at leaves and merge

$$
F_v=F_LP_R+F_RP_L.
$$

The root is $f$, in $O(M(n)\log n)$. Duplicated points make
$P'(x_i)=0$; either reject inconsistent input or use Hermite interpolation.

For a polynomial of degree at most $n$ known at the consecutive points
$0,\ldots,n$,
evaluation at arbitrary $t$ can be done in $O(n)$ using prefix/suffix products
and
$$
f(t)=\sum_i y_i\frac{\prod_{j\ne i}(t-j)}{i!(-1)^{n-i}(n-i)!}.
$$

## 5. Taylor shift

Find coefficients of $f(x+c)$. Since

$$
[x^k]f(x+c)=\sum_{i\ge k}a_i{i\choose k}c^{i-k},
$$

multiply by $k!$ and rewrite as a convolution of reversed
$A_i=a_i i!$ with $B_j=c^{j}/j!$, then divide the result by $k!$.
This is $O(M(n))$, assuming factorials are invertible.

## 6. Product of many polynomials

Use a priority queue or divide-and-conquer product tree, multiplying similar
degrees first. For total output degree $N$, balanced multiplication is typically
$O(M(N)\log k)$. Always truncate to the maximum requested degree; for knapsack
factors this can save orders of magnitude.

## 7. Failure checklist and sources

- Transform length must divide `MOD-1`; it must also cover `a.size+b.size-1`.
- Normalize negative residues before NTT.
- CRT primes must support the same transform length.
- Polynomial inverse requires nonzero constant coefficient; division instead
  relies on the divisor's leading coefficient.
- Multipoint interpolation requires distinct points.
